ABSTRACT: Three-component reductive dicarbofunctionaliza-
tion reactions of 1,3-enynes have been rarely reported because of
the intricate control of chemo- and regioselectivity required,
coupled with a limited understanding of radical and catalytic
species involved. Herein, we report a nickel-catalyzed reductive
1,4-alkylarylation method for 1,3-enynes to yield tri- and
tetrasubstituted allenes using readily accessible alkyl and aryl
iodides, featuring a simple operational protocol and mild reaction
conditions. In our mechanistic studies, the formation of a
propargyl/allenyl radical was substantiated by the isolation of a
propargyl dimer, the detection of the corresponding TEMPO−
radical adduct, and radical probe experiments. Two reduced L
2
NiAr complexes, expected to act as catalytic intermediates, were
generated and characterized by EPR spectroscopy as Ni
I
complexes. The stoichiometric reaction of L
2
Ni(p-NCC
6
H

) with 1,3-enyne
and alkyl iodide showed conversion into the corresponding propargyl dimer and allene, suggesting that the reaction encompasses the
same key mechanistic steps as the catalytic reaction, i.e., activation of alkyl iodide, generation of a propargyl/allenyl radical, and
selective coupling of this radical with the aryl component.
KEYWORDS: allenes, (aryl)nickel(I) complexes, 1,3-enynes, nickel catalysis, radical relay, reductive coupling, three-component reaction
1. INTRODUCTION
Allenes are cumulated dienes, which have garnered considerable
attention in pharmaceutical science and in the synthetic
community because of their distinct biological activity and
chemical reactivity.
1
Prototropic and sigmatropic rearrange-
ments, as well as substitution and elimination reactions,
represent classic methods for the synthesis of allenes.
1,2
However, these methods often involve laborious steps for
preparing activated substrates and require harsh reaction
conditions, particularly when aiming to synthesize multi-
substituted allenes. In this regard, the catalytic functionalization
of readily accessible 1,3-enynes to afford multisubstituted allenes
has gained attraction as an efficient and practical synthetic
approach.
3
For instance, the Hoveyda, Engle, and Ge groups
independently reported CuH-catalyzed hydroboration reactions
of 1,3-enynes to give allenyl boronates.
4
Moreover, catalytic
hydrosilylation, hydrogenation, hydroalkylation, and hydro-
arylation reactions of 1,3-enynes using hydride sources have
been extensively studied, which likely proceed through metal-
hydride complexes generated in situ.
5
Unlike hydrofunctionalization, dicarbofunctionalization of
1,3-enynes, which directly forms two C−C bonds, has emerged
as a powerful synthetic approach for the efficient synthesis of
allenes. However, the polar approach via allenyl anion species
typically involves the use of organolithium reagents, which often
limits the tolerance for functional groups and necessitates
cryogenic cooling (Scheme 1A).
6
Recently, there has been
remarkable progress in radical-involved dicarbofunctionaliza-
tion of unsaturated systems, including 1,3-enynes, by merging
single-electron transfer processes and transition-metal cataly-
sis.
7,8
Radical-based redox-neutral 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization
of 1,3-enynes has been demonstrated (Scheme 1B). These
methods offer the advantage of efficient twofold C−C bond
formation.
Cross-electrophile coupling (XEC) reactions of π systems,
utilizing readily available organic (pseudo)halides, have recently
garnered significant attention in the synthetic community. This
is attributed to their mild reaction conditions, simple operations,
and improved functional group compatibility.
9
The application
of the XEC approach to three-component reductive difunction-
alization has been demonstrated for alkenes as the conjunctive
platform.
10
High levels of chemo- and regioselectivity were
achieved by utilizing activated alkenes to enable the philicity-

present in Ni-catalyzed reactions under reductive conditions,
which may generate NiH species through the oxidative addition
of alkyl halide and subsequent β-hydrogen elimination.
14
Recent
examples of XEC reactions of 1,3-enynes utilized photo-
chemistry or electrochemistry for electrophile activation, in
addition to Ni catalysis.
8a,15
The reactivity of different sites of
the 1,3-enyne substrate was examined through DFT calcu-
lations.
15b
However, despite the progress in the development of
reductive dicarbofunctionalization of unsaturated systems, the
mechanistic understanding of the reactivity of radical
intermediates and catalytically active species remains limited.
Herein, we report an operationally straightforward Ni-
catalyzed reductive 1,4-alkylarylation of conjugated 1,3-enynes
using a metal reducing agent as a complementary synthetic route
to furnish tri- or tetrasubstituted allenes (Scheme 1C). In studies
on related reductive Ni catalysis with unsaturated substra-
tes,
12c,13b
reduced Ni complexes such as L
2
NiX and L
2
NiAr were
proposed to initiate the reaction through the activation of alkyl
halide to generate an alkyl radical. In the three-component XEC
reaction described here, an alkyl radical generated in situ may
react with the 1,3-enyne to give a propargyl/allenyl radical
(Scheme 1D). We present mechanistic evidence of the presence
and involvement of a propargyl/allenyl radical as an
intermediate in this reaction. The excellent chemo- and
regioselectivity observed in the allene product formation
suggests selective coupling of this radical with the aryl
component. Furthermore, we report the generation, character-
ization, and reactivity of reduced L
2
NiAr complexes (Scheme
1D), demonstrating that they can function as catalytic
intermediates in XEC reactions of 1,3-enynes.
2. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
2.1. Reaction Optimization. Catalytic 1,4-dicarbofunc-
tionalization of 1,3-enyne 1 was conducted using para-
iodobenzonitrile (2) and tert-butyl iodide (3) as model aryl
and alkyl electrophiles. After extensive screening of reaction
parameters (see also the Supporting Information, Section 3), the
optimized reaction conditions resulted in the formation of
tetrasubstituted allene 4 as a single regioisomer in 88% yield
(Table 1, entry 1). The combination of NiCl
2
(py)
4
and 2,2′-
bipyridine (L1) turned out to be the optimal precatalyst (entries
2−8). It is of note that the 1,2-difunctionalized regioisomer was
also not observed with ligands L2−L6. Substituting Zn or
TDAE for Mn as the reducing agent resulted in decreased yields
(entries 9 and 10). The absence of TBAI significantly
diminished the yield of the product (entry 11). Presumably,
TBAI facilitates the electron transfer from Mn by improving
homogeneity.
16
The use of TMSCl did not improve the yield
(entry 12).
17
The reaction conditions were further optimized by
reducing the amount of Mn to 1.5 equiv and that of TBAI to 0.75
equiv, while shortening the reaction time to 1 h (entry 13 and
Supporting Information, Section 3).
2.2. Reaction Scope. With the optimized conditions, we
examined 1,3-enynes with a diverse range of substituents (R
1
, R
2
,
and R
3
), as depicted in Table 2. Various aryl substituents in R
3
position exhibited excellent tolerance toward the reductive 1,4-
alkylarylation reaction affording the tetrasubstituted allene
products. Good to excellent yields (68−95%) were observed
regardless of the electronic nature of the aryl substituents of 4, 5,
and 7−12, which indicates the involvement of a radical
intermediate rather than anionic or cationic intermediates.
However, the conversion of a 1,3-enyne with an ortho-methyl
substituent in the R
3
arene ring required an extended reaction
time to yield allene 6 in 47% yield, presumably because of steric
hindrance. Interestingly, symmetric bis(allene) 13 was also
obtained through double 1,4-alkylarylation in 38% yield.
8g
Fused arenes were also incorporated giving 14 and 15 in 88 and
64% yield, respectively. The sterically encumbering 9-phenan-
threnyl substituent showed slightly diminished efficiency.
Among heteroaromatic substituents, the 3-pyridyl moiety
provided product 16 in 53% yield. The 2- or 3-thienyl group
afforded the corresponding allenes 17 and 18 in yields of 90 and
93%, respectively. To our delight, the desired allene products
19−21 and 24 were readily obtained in 56−81% yield from 1,3-
enynes with alkyl, chloroalkyl, cyanoalkyl, and benzyl sub-
stituents in the position of R
3
. 1,3-Enynes with acidic hydroxy
and amide groups were well tolerated to give the allenes 22 and
23 in yields of 49 and 80%, respectively.
Reactions of 1,3-enynes with various R
2
substituents
furnished the corresponding allene products in 33−79% yield.
Substrates with a phenyl substituent in R
2
underwent the desired
1,4-alkylarylation reaction to generate the allenes 25−27 in 44−
79% yield. Reactions of 1,3-enynes with alkyl substituents in R
2
position delivered the corresponding products in moderate
yields (48 and 57% for 28 and 29, respectively). The formation
of 23 and 28 highlights the synthetic utility of our method as a
rapid approach to allene precursors of heterocyclic compounds
by intramolecular cyclization.
1b,8e
The reaction of a mono-
substituted 1,3-enyne (S30) gave the desired allene in a
diminished yield (39% for 30) along with the 1,2-difunction-
alization product (7%). The decreased regioselectivity in this
reaction suggests that it depends on the steric effect of the R
2
substituent (Supporting Information, Section 4). Furthermore,
the dicarbofunctionalization of trisubstituted 1,3-enynes was
examined. The reactions using a fused-cyclic 1,3-enyne and a
triphenyl-substituted 1,3-enyne yielded allene products 31 and
32 in yields of 47 and 33%, respectively. Notably, allene 31,
having an exocyclic double bond, was obtained as a single
diastereomer, but a reduced diastereomeric ratio was observed
for unfused allene 32.
Next, we evaluated the aryl iodide scope in this protocol.
When para-iodobenzonitrile was replaced with meta-iodoben-
zonitrile, the reaction afforded allene 34 in a yield similar to that
of 4 (86 vs 88%). However, when ortho-iodobenzonitrile was
used, the yield of the allene (33) was drastically reduced to 15%,
indicating a detrimental steric effect of the ortho substituent.
Ester, formyl, and acetyl moieties were compatible with the
reaction conditions (35−37, 52−88% yield). We also
investigated F- and CF
3
-substituted aryl iodides, which find
extensive application in pharmaceutical science and materials
chemistry. These substrates successfully underwent the
reactions leading to the formation of allenes 38, 40, 41, and
45−47 in 47−80% yield. When we tried to use electron-neutral
or electron-rich aryl iodides in this method, the reactions
resulted in complex mixtures and the desired allene products
were not observed (Figure S1). An aryl iodide substituted with
both an electron-donating methoxy group and an electron-
withdrawing cyano group was converted into allene 39 in 89%
yield. Although electron-deficient aryl iodides showed better
yields, the formation of 39 from this aryl iodide implies that the
reaction is not limited to aryl iodides bearing only electron-
withdrawing groups. Halide compatibility was tested using 1-
halo-4-iodobenzenes (F-, Cl-, Br-, and I-substituted aryl
iodides). 1-Chloro-4-iodobenzene gave allene 42 in 49% yield.
1-Bromo-4-iodobenzene showed good Br/I selectivity to give

2.3. Evidence of a Propargyl/Allenyl Radical Inter-
mediate. Upon activation of alkyl iodide by the active Ni
catalyst, the addition of an alkyl radical to a 1,3-enyne may take
place at multiple sites.
15b
Thus, depending on the position of the
radical addition, a diverse array of radicals can be formed. To
confirm the presence of a radical intermediate derived from the
1,3-enyne substrate and to elucidate its identity, we carried out
several experiments. The reaction of 1,3-enyne 1 and alkyl iodide
3 in the absence of aryl iodide afforded product 57, which was
isolated and accounted for 38% conversion of 1 (Scheme 2A).
Its structure was determined by X-ray crystallography. The
formation of 57 is explained by the recombination of two

The observation of the propargyl dimer 57 prompted us to
probe the propargyl/allenyl radical further. While butylated

of 1 (yield of 4, 85%), 9,10-dihydroanthracene (DHA) and 1,1-

To elucidate the involvement of a free propargyl/allenyl
radical in the catalytic reaction, we introduced radical probe
substituents in the R
2

either the propargyl radical C(sp

the active Ni catalyst. Under standard reaction conditions, the
use of a 1,3-enyne with a cyclopropyl group installed in the
position of R
2
(58, Scheme 2C) afforded allene 59 and the ring-
opened enyne 59′.

inseparable mixture (48% total yield) with a ratio of 1:1.2, as
determined by
1

These results suggest that the propargyl/allenyl radical is an
intermediate in the catalytic reaction and that it undergoes
coupling with the aryl component either at the allenyl radical
center (B) to give 59 or at the ring-opened alkyl radical center
(C) to give 59′. No product was observed from coupling at the
propargyl radical center (A), as was the case for other 1,3-enynes
examined (Table 2). In contrast, standard reactions using a 1,3-
enyne with a ring-closing or ring-opening radical probe installed
in R
3

same radical probe (cyclopropyl group) as enyne 58, the

(Scheme 3), was not observed at all. These observations indicate

derived from 58 (R
2
= cyclopropyl) is comparable with the rate
of ring-opening and coupling of C but that the consumption rate
of the propargyl/allenyl radical derived from 60 (R
3
=
cyclopropyl) is faster than the rate of ring-opening and coupling
of D.
2.4. Generation, Characterization, and Stoichiometric
Reactions of Reduced L
2
NiAr Complexes. The isolation of
the propargyl dimer (57), the detection of a TEMPO−
propargyl/allenyl radical adduct by high-resolution mass
spectrometry, and the radical probe experiments together
indicate the intermediacy of a propargyl/allenyl radical (Scheme
4). The formation of this radical can be explained by the reaction
of 1 with the tert-butyl radical, which may be generated from the
reaction of 3 with a reduced Ni complex, such as L
2
NiAr or
L

reactions of other reduced Ni complexes with alkyl iodides.

scope studies, we hypothesize that the propargyl/allenyl radical

3. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we have developed a nickel-catalyzed reductive 1,4-
alkylarylation method for the catalytic conversion of 1,3-enynes
into tri- or tetrasubstituted allenes. The selective transformation
of conjugated π systems, including 1,3-enynes, has remained a
challenging topic because of the presence of multiple active sites
suitable for coupling reactions. Here, the conversion of 1,3-
enynes into allenes was achieved using alkyl and aryl iodides and
without the need for substrate preactivation or directing groups.
Our mechanistic investigation revealed a propargyl/allenyl
radical as an intermediate in the catalytic reaction. We also
investigated the reactivity of L
2
NiAr complexes, which are
expected to be involved in this reaction and in related Ni-
catalyzed reductive difunctionalization reactions of unsaturated
substrates. In particular, the complexes Ni(L5)(p-NCC
6
H
4
)
and Ni(L5)(Ph) were generated in situ and characterized as Ni
I
complexes. The reaction of Ni(L5)(p-NCC
6
H
4
) with alkyl
iodide and 1,3-enyne formed the propargyl radical dimer and the
allene product. This result indicates that this complex is a
possible intermediate in the catalytic reaction described here
and that it can promote the activation of alkyl iodide, the
generation of the propargyl/allenyl radical, and the selective
coupling of this radical with the aryl component. By contrast, the
reaction of Ni(L5)(Ph), derived from the catalytically inactive
phenyl iodide, formed only the propargyl radical dimer but not
the allene. These results may suggest an electronic effect of the
aryl component in the XEC reaction and offer a rationale for the
scope of aryl iodides in the catalytic reaction. We anticipate that
this work contributes to the expansion of the territory of
conjunctive platforms for selectivity-controlled reductive three-
component difunctionalization reactions.
